## 5a. Three questions about the shape set

### Does a `unimodal` peak at the edge of the scale become `monotone`?

Within the measured window, yes — visually. A bump centred at `MID_HI` shows only
its rising half, which reads as a monotone increase. The two are not the same
function (a half-bump curves, a `monotone` fit is a straight line), but at
realistic noise levels they are not reliably distinguishable.

A monotone curve means **no reference point** — Weber's law operating with no
categorical structure anywhere. It maps to zero.

The competing reading is that it marks a reference point sitting *outside* the
measured window, showing only one flank. With midpoints running from `MID_LO` to
`MID_HI` that window now spans all but the outermost 0.2 stars at each end of the
rating scale, so a reference point would have to sit almost exactly on 1.0 or 5.0
to produce it. The ambiguity is not eliminated — a reference point at the very
bottom of the scale still leaves a decaying flank that can read as a slope — but
it is confined to a corner of the scale, and the reference points the study is
designed to find sit at 2.5 and 3.5, deep in the interior. The simulation
therefore generates monotone participants as a straight Weber slope and counts
them as zero.

## 5b. Peak width: a non-technical account

This section gives a non-technical account of `PEAK_W`. §5d gives the formal
derivation.

### Reference points vary from occasion to occasion

Consider a participant applying the rule **"4 stars and up is good; below that,
not"**. Their reference point is at 4.

But people are not machines. On Monday they might accept 3.9. On Tuesday they
might hold out for 4.1. Their line drifts around a little from moment to moment.

**How much that line drifts is the whole story.** Some people are very
consistent — their line sits within a hair of 4.0 every time. Others are wobbly,
landing anywhere between 3.6 and 4.4 depending on mood.

`PEAK_W` is simply **a number describing how much a person's line wobbles**. If
their line typically moves by about 0.3 stars, `PEAK_W` is 0.3. That is all it
is. It is a badly chosen name for a simple idea.

### Why reference-point variability produces a hump

Your task shows two products a fixed distance apart and asks how different they
feel.

| the pair | what the person thinks | their answer |
|---|---|---|
| 4.5 and 4.7 | both comfortably "good", same side of the line | small |
| 2.0 and 2.2 | both comfortably "not good", same side again | small |
| **3.9 and 4.1** | **one is a yes, the other a no** | **large** |

So answers are **large near the line and small away from it**. Plot the answers
against where the pair sits on the scale and you get a hump centred on the
person's line. Finding that hump is what this whole document is about.

### Why the hump is smooth rather than a spike

If the line never moved — always exactly 4.0 — then only pairs straddling exactly
4.0 would feel different, and you would get a razor-thin spike.

But the line does move:

- a pair at **3.9 / 4.1** straddles the line almost every time, so it nearly
  always feels different
- a pair at **3.7 / 3.9** straddles it only on days the line drifts low, so it
  *sometimes* feels different
- a pair at **3.0 / 3.2** essentially never straddles it

The hump therefore **fades out gradually** as you move away from the line, and
how fast it fades is exactly how much the line wobbles. A wobbly person gets a
**wide, gentle** hump; a consistent person gets a **narrow, tall** one.

That is where the bell shape comes from. It is not an assumption bolted on for
convenience — it falls out of the wobble. §5c checks this by computing the curve
exactly, without assuming any bell shape, and comparing.

### The two-reference-point case

Someone with a neutral zone has **two** lines: "below 3 is bad, above 4 is good,
in between is neither." Two lines give two humps, one sitting at each line. That
is the `bimodal` shape.

### Why narrow neutral zones are unresolvable

Put those together.

**Two lines far apart** — say 3.0 and 4.5 — give two clearly separate humps with
a clear dip between them, and the two are readily distinguished.

**Two lines close together** — say 3.4 and 3.6, each wobbling by 0.3 stars — give
humps wide enough to swallow the gap between them. They blur into one blob, and
there is **no dip at all**. Not a faint dip needing more data; no dip.

The rule: **the two lines must be roughly twice as far apart as the wobble.**

| if the wobble is... | the narrowest neutral zone you can detect is... |
|---|---|
| 0.15 stars | about 0.3 stars |
| 0.30 stars | about 0.55 stars |
| 0.45 stars | about 0.8 stars |

Measured neutral zones on a 5-point scale are **0.6-0.8 stars**. If people's
lines wobble by around 0.3, this design sits right on the edge of what it can
see — which is why the power numbers in §8 and §13 stay stubborn no matter what
is changed about the analysis.

::: {.callout-important}
## The quantity to estimate in piloting

**How much does a person's line wobble?** Everything follows from it, and it has
not been measured yet.

Fit the one-hump shape to pilot data and read off the width — it comes out of the
fit automatically, as the fourth fitted parameter.

- near **0.15** — this design works comfortably
- near **0.30** — borderline; it works, but barely
- near **0.45** — most real neutral zones are invisible to this task, and the
  direct-question design in §14 is the way to go
:::

## 5c. Two design parameters

Two natural ideas for improving matters. Both were simulated by
`pair_gap_and_repeats.py`, which writes the CSVs read below. **Both turn out to
make no useful difference**, and the reasons are worth understanding.

### Effect of the pair gap

You currently show pairs 0.2 stars apart (1.0 versus 1.2). Would a wider gap
help?

It is genuinely a trade, because the gap changes **two** things at once:

- a wider gap gives **more signal** — bigger differences are easier to report
  consistently, so the hump is taller
- but it also **blurs the hump wider**, because a wide pair straddles the line
  from further away

```{python}
#| label: tbl-pair-gap
#| tbl-cap: "Type II error (lower is better) for three neutral-zone widths. Both the hump height and the hump width are derived from the wobble model rather than assumed, so widening the gap raises them together. 300 people per cell, so the margin is about +/- 5.7 points."

import os
if os.path.exists('pair_gap_power.csv'):
    pg = pd.read_csv('pair_gap_power.csv')
    display(pg.pivot_table(
        index=['pair gap', 'hump width', 'hump height (slider pts)'],
        columns='neutral zone', values='Type II (%)'))
else:
    print("Run pair_gap_and_repeats.py first.")
```

**The two effects cancel almost exactly.** Going from a 0.2 gap to a 0.6 gap
raises the hump from 30 to 41 slider points — a real gain in signal — but widens
it from 0.28 to 0.34 stars, and the error rates barely move. For a 0.8-star
neutral zone the Type II error runs 35, 38, 33, 41, 44 across the whole range,
which is inside the margin of error.

**So there is no meaningful difference between 0.3 and 0.4, or indeed between
0.2 and 0.5.** Keep 0.2 if it is already piloted; the choice is not load-bearing.
If anything the widest gaps are slightly worse, so do not go above about 0.4.

### Effect of repeated measurement

This is the more interesting question, because it depends on **which kind of
noise you are fighting**. There are two, and they are not the same:

| | what it is | do repeats fix it? |
|---|---|---|
| **Slider noise** | You know what you think, but the slider lands imprecisely | **Yes** — averaging cancels it |
| **Reference-point wobble** | Your line genuinely moves from moment to moment | **No** |

Repeats fix the first and not the second. The reason is that the wobble is not
scatter *around* the hump — the wobble is **what gives the hump its shape**.
Asking the same pair repeatedly gives you a better measurement of an already
blurred quantity. Measuring a blurry photograph more carefully does not sharpen
the photograph.

And repeats are not free: at a fixed number of judgments, asking each pair three
times means only a third as many distinct midpoints.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-repeats
#| tbl-cap: "Total judgments held fixed at 45, split different ways. More repeats mean less noise per midpoint but fewer distinct midpoints. 300 people per cell, margin about +/- 5.7 points."

if os.path.exists('repeats_power.csv'):
    rp = pd.read_csv('repeats_power.csv')
    display(rp.pivot_table(
        index=['times each pair is asked', 'distinct midpoints',
               'effective noise per midpoint'],
        columns='neutral zone', values=['Type I (%)', 'Type II (%)']))
else:
    print("Run pair_gap_and_repeats.py first.")
```

**The trade is a wash up to about three repeats, then it turns bad.** For a
0.8-star zone the Type II error is 35, 34, 35, 41 as repeats go 1, 2, 3, 5 — flat
until five repeats leaves only nine distinct midpoints, at which point there are
too few points to describe a two-humped curve (the same collapse as the coarse
scale in §15).

And repeats do not sharpen the estimate of the wobble either:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-width-bias
#| tbl-cap: "The fitted hump width, again at a fixed 45-judgment budget. If repeats reduced the wobble, the fitted width would shrink as repeats increase. It does not."

if os.path.exists('width_bias.csv'):
    display(pd.read_csv('width_bias.csv').set_index('times each pair is asked'))
else:
    print("Run pair_gap_and_repeats.py first.")
```

The fitted width stays within a few percent of the truth at every setting. That
is the simulation confirming the conceptual point: **repeats measure the hump
more precisely; they do not narrow it.**

### Allocation of a fixed judgment budget

The sharpest version of the question, with the **total judgments held exactly
equal** in each comparison so nothing is confounded with effort.
`allocation_test.py` runs it at 600 people per cell.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-allocation
#| tbl-cap: "Equal budgets, split two ways. 600 people per cell, so the margin on any single rate is +/- 4.0 points and on the A-minus-B difference +/- 5.7 points. A negative difference favours repeating pairs; positive favours more unique pairs."

if os.path.exists('allocation_results.csv'):
    al = pd.read_csv('allocation_results.csv')
    display(al[['total judgments', 'neutral zone', 'A: pairs x reps', 'A Type II (%)',
                'B: pairs x reps', 'B Type II (%)', 'Type II: A minus B']]
            .set_index(['total judgments', 'neutral zone']))
else:
    print("Run allocation_test.py first.")
```

**It is a tie.** Every one of the nine differences sits inside the ±5.7-point
margin, and the average across them is +1.3 points — a whisker in favour of more
unique pairs, far too small to act on. Choose on practical grounds: participant
fatigue, how many distinct midpoints your rating granularity actually supports
(§15), or whether you want the replicates for the reason below.

### Partial replication

A better idea than either extreme: ask **30 distinct pairs, 10 of them twice**,
for 40 judgments. `hybrid_design.py` tests it.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-hybrid-power
#| tbl-cap: "Partial replication at a fixed 40-judgment budget. Cells are Type II error. 500 people per cell, margin about +/- 4.4 points."

if os.path.exists('hybrid_power.csv'):
    hp = pd.read_csv('hybrid_power.csv')
    display(hp.pivot_table(index=['design', 'distinct midpoints'],
                           columns='neutral zone', values='Type II (%)'))
else:
    print("Run hybrid_design.py first.")
```

Power is **identical** across every allocation — as §5c has now established three
separate ways. So the hybrid costs nothing. The reason to want it is different,
and it is a good one.

**Two answers to the same pair differ only by noise**, whatever the true curve
looks like. That gives a **model-free estimate of slider noise** — the `SLIDER_SD`
that the whole document depends on and that you would otherwise have to infer
from residuals, which conflates real noise with the curve model being slightly
wrong.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-hybrid-noise
#| tbl-cap: "How precisely the repeated pairs recover the slider noise. The true value is 12.0 slider points. Even 10 repeated pairs pins it down to roughly +/- 15%."

if os.path.exists('hybrid_noise.csv'):
    display(pd.read_csv('hybrid_noise.csv').set_index('design'))
else:
    print("Run hybrid_design.py first.")
```

Ten repeated pairs recover the slider noise to within about 15%, and thirteen to
within 13%. Since **`PEAK_AMP / SLIDER_SD` is the master parameter of this whole
document** (§4g), getting its denominator cleanly, for free, in the main study
rather than a separate pilot, is worth ten judgments.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A limitation of the replicate-based check

Replicates should in principle also give a **lack-of-fit test**: if the residuals
around the fitted curve are much larger than the noise the replicates imply, the
bump shape is wrong for that person. It would be a way to check §5d against real
data instead of assuming it.

Tested, it does not work at this noise level:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-hybrid-lackfit
#| tbl-cap: "Lack-of-fit test with 10 repeated pairs. If it worked, the triangular-peak row would show a clearly larger ratio and a higher flag rate. It does not."

if os.path.exists('hybrid_lackfit.csv'):
    display(pd.read_csv('hybrid_lackfit.csv').set_index('truth'))
else:
    print("Run hybrid_design.py first.")
```

Both rows give a ratio of 1.02 and flag rates within the margin of each other.
This is **consistent with §11.1**, which found that swapping Gaussian peaks for
triangular ones barely changes the classification: at `PEAK_AMP / SLIDER_SD` of
2.5 the difference between the two shapes is simply buried in the noise. The test
correctly reports no detectable misfit, because there is none to detect. Do not
plan on validating the peak shape this way unless your pilot comes back with a
much quieter slider.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Recommendation

**30 distinct pairs with 10 of them repeated, 40 judgments in total.** Power is
indistinguishable from any other split, it clears the ~15 distinct-midpoint floor
from §15 comfortably, and the ten repeats hand you a clean, model-free
measurement of the slider noise you need for every other table in this document.
:::


::: {.callout-tip}
## Summary of §5c

Neither knob moves the error rates. The pair gap is a wash, repeats are a wash
until they start hurting, and splitting a fixed budget between the two is a wash
as well.

That is genuinely useful, because it says the levers are elsewhere: the wobble
itself (a property of the participants, and a quantity to be estimated), and the
choice of task (§14).

But it also means replication is **free**, and free is worth taking when it buys
you something. Use the hybrid: **30 distinct pairs, 10 repeated**. You lose no
power, you stay well clear of the distinct-midpoint floor, and you walk away with
a model-free measurement of the slider noise that every other table here
depends on.
:::


## 5d. Derivation of the bump shape

`PEAK_W` is not a free-floating smoothing knob. It falls out of a specific model
of what a reference point *is*, and that model tells you what the peak shape
should be. This section derives it and checks it.

### Origin of the peak

Suppose a person has one reference point at rating `b`. They do not apply it perfectly:
on any given occasion their effective reference-point wobbles a little, so whether a
rating counts as "above" is a **probability** rather than a certainty. Write that
as a cumulative Gaussian with standard deviation `sigma` — small `sigma` means a
crisp reference point, large `sigma` a fuzzy one. This is the standard signal-detection
assumption.

Now show them a pair of ratings `delta` apart, centred on midpoint `m`. The two
members feel categorically different exactly when they get **different labels**,
which has probability

`P(different) = P(above | upper) * P(below | lower) + P(above | lower) * P(below | upper)`

Nothing about that expression is Gaussian-shaped by assumption. So compute it
exactly and see what shape comes out.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-theory-shape
#| tbl-cap: "The exact categorical-difference curve, computed with no bump assumed, then fitted with the Gaussian bump this document uses. R-squared of 1.000 means the Gaussian is not an approximation of convenience -- it is what the categorisation model actually produces. Two different reference-point models are tried, to check the result is not an artefact of assuming a normal reference point."

from scipy.stats import norm, logistic as _logistic

THEORY_SIGMA, THEORY_DELTA = 0.30, 0.20
_tx = np.linspace(MID_LO, MID_HI, 801)
_g1 = lambda x, a, A, m, w: a + A * np.exp(-0.5 * ((x - m) / w) ** 2)
_g2 = lambda x, a, A, m1, m2, w: a + A * (np.exp(-0.5 * ((x - m1) / w) ** 2)
                                          + np.exp(-0.5 * ((x - m2) / w) ** 2))
def _r2(y, yh):
    return 1 - np.sum((y - yh) ** 2) / np.sum((y - y.mean()) ** 2)

_cdf_probit = lambda x, b, s: norm.cdf((x - b) / s)
_cdf_logit  = lambda x, b, s: _logistic.cdf((x - b) / (s * np.sqrt(3) / np.pi))

def _pdiff1(b, s, cdf, delta=THEORY_DELTA):
    lo, hi = cdf(_tx - delta / 2, b, s), cdf(_tx + delta / 2, b, s)
    return hi * (1 - lo) + lo * (1 - hi)

rows = []
for nm, cdf in (("probit (cumulative normal)", _cdf_probit),
                ("logit (logistic)", _cdf_logit)):
    y = _pdiff1(PEAK_CENTRE, THEORY_SIGMA, cdf)
    po, _ = curve_fit(_g1, _tx, y, p0=[0, y.max(), PEAK_CENTRE, THEORY_SIGMA])
    rows.append({'reference-point model': nm,
                 'R^2 of Gaussian bump fit': round(_r2(y, _g1(_tx, *po)), 5),
                 'fitted PEAK_W': round(po[3], 4),
                 "participant's reference-point SD": THEORY_SIGMA,
                 'ratio': round(po[3] / THEORY_SIGMA, 3)})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('reference-point model')
```

**So `PEAK_W` is the standard deviation of the person's reference point** — how
much their reference point wobbles from occasion to occasion. It is a real
psychological quantity with units of stars, not a curve-fitting convenience. And
the Gaussian bump is not an approximation you tolerate; it is what this model
produces, to four decimal places, under either reference-point model.

### The two-reference-point model

The `bimodal` shape adds two bumps together. That is a *modelling choice* on top
of the derivation above, so it needs its own check. A person with two reference points
has **three** categories, and the exact probability that two ratings get different
labels is not obviously a sum of two bumps.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-theory-two
#| tbl-cap: "Exact three-category difference curve, fitted with the sum-of-two-Gaussians used by the bimodal shape. It also recovers the neutral-zone width: compare the fitted gap against the true gap. Note the upward bias at the narrowest gap, where the two bumps overlap heavily."

def _pdiff2(b1, b2, s, delta=THEORY_DELTA):
    def probs(x):
        p_lo = 1 - norm.cdf((x - b1) / s)
        p_hi = norm.cdf((x - b2) / s)
        return np.vstack([p_lo, np.clip(1 - p_lo - p_hi, 0, 1), p_hi])
    P1, P2 = probs(_tx - delta / 2), probs(_tx + delta / 2)
    return 1 - np.sum(P1 * P2, axis=0)

rows = []
for gap in (0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.4):
    b1, b2 = PEAK_CENTRE - gap / 2, PEAK_CENTRE + gap / 2
    y = _pdiff2(b1, b2, THEORY_SIGMA)
    try:
        po, _ = curve_fit(_g2, _tx, y, p0=[0, y.max(), b1, b2, THEORY_SIGMA], maxfev=20000)
        rows.append({'true neutral zone': gap,
                     'R^2 of 2-bump fit': round(_r2(y, _g2(_tx, *po)), 5),
                     'fitted PEAK_W': round(po[4], 4),
                     'recovered zone width': round(abs(po[3] - po[2]), 4)})
    except Exception:
        rows.append({'true neutral zone': gap, 'R^2 of 2-bump fit': np.nan,
                     'fitted PEAK_W': np.nan, 'recovered zone width': np.nan})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('true neutral zone')
```

Both the shape and the recovered width hold. The only wrinkle is at a 0.4-star
zone, where the fitted width comes out about 15% too wide — the two bumps overlap
so heavily that the fit cannot fully separate them. That is the same resolution
limit as §5, showing up as bias rather than as failure.

### A resolution floor set by reference-point variability

Here is the part that matters for planning. §5 says two reference points are only
visible as two humps when they are more than `2 * PEAK_W` apart. We now know
`PEAK_W` is roughly the participant's reference-point SD. So:

**the narrowest neutral zone this task can ever resolve is about twice the
fuzziness of the participant's own reference points.**

That is a fact about the participant, not about your sample size, your
classifier, or your rating scale. The one design knob that touches it is the
**pair gap `delta`**.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-theory-delta
#| tbl-cap: "The person is held fixed (reference-point SD 0.30); only the pair gap changes. A wider gap buys signal but broadens the peak, which raises the narrowest neutral zone you can resolve. Signal is expressed relative to a 0.2-star gap."

rows = []
_A0 = None
for d in (0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00):
    y = _pdiff1(PEAK_CENTRE, THEORY_SIGMA, _cdf_probit, delta=d)
    po, _ = curve_fit(_g1, _tx, y, p0=[0, y.max(), PEAK_CENTRE, THEORY_SIGMA])
    A, w = po[1], po[3]
    if d == 0.20:
        _A0 = A
    rows.append({'pair gap (delta)': d, 'peak width': round(w, 4),
                 'width / reference-point SD': round(w / THEORY_SIGMA, 3),
                 'narrowest zone resolvable': round(2 * w, 3),
                 'signal (raw)': round(A, 4)})
df_d = pd.DataFrame(rows)
df_d['signal vs delta=0.2'] = (df_d['signal (raw)'] / _A0).round(3)
df_d.drop(columns='signal (raw)').set_index('pair gap (delta)')
```

Three observations follow.

**There is a hard floor.** As the pair gap shrinks, the peak width stops falling
at about `0.9 * sigma`. So the narrowest resolvable neutral zone is about
`1.8 * sigma` — around **0.54 stars if reference-point SD is 0.30** — and no choice of
`delta` gets below it.

**Your current gap of 0.2 is close to optimal, but slightly conservative.** Going
from 0.2 to 0.3 or 0.4 raises the resolution limit only from 0.56 to 0.61 stars
while increasing the signal by 7-17%. Since `PEAK_AMP / SLIDER_SD` is the master
parameter for power, that is probably a good trade.

**Gaps much beyond `delta = sigma` are counterproductive.** At `delta = 0.8` the peak has widened
to 0.45 and the resolution limit has moved out to 0.78 stars, which is wider than
the neutral zones you measured on a 5-point scale.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Implication for the pair gap

Keep the pair gap at or a little below the reference-point fuzziness: **`delta <= sigma`**.
Within that range widening the gap is nearly free signal. Past it you start
trading away the resolution you need.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Assumptions not addressed by this derivation

Three elements remain assumptions rather than results:

- **The slider is linear in perceived difference.** The derivation gives a
  *probability* of a categorical difference; the doc treats the 0-100 slider as
  proportional to it. A compressive or expansive response mapping would distort
  the peak.
- **The baseline is the non-categorical part.** `BASELINE` stands in for ordinary
  nominal-distance sensitivity, which exists whether or not a reference point is nearby.
  Theory says it should carry a Weber tilt (`BASE_SLOPE`), which the config
  defaults to zero — see §11.6.
- **Peak height and width are drawn independently.** In the derivation they are
  mildly coupled: a sharper reference point gives a slightly taller peak, about 1.17x
  going from `sigma = 0.30` down to 0.15. That is smaller than `JITTER_AMP`, so
  treating them as independent is a minor sin, but it is a sin.
:::


## 6. The classifier

Four candidate shapes are fitted to each person's data by least squares and the
one with the best **AICc** wins — AICc rather than AIC because a person
contributing 20 points is firmly in small-sample territory. AICc rewards fitting
the dots well and penalises using more parameters to do it, so the flexible
`bimodal` shape has to earn its two extra parameters.

::: {.callout-important}
## Convergence tolerance

Fitting the 5-parameter `bimodal` model to a person who has **no peak at all** is
an *unidentifiable* problem: once the fitted amplitude collapses towards zero,
the two peak-location parameters stop affecting the fit entirely, the optimiser
has no gradient to follow, and it grinds through its whole evaluation budget
before giving up. Measured cost of a single bimodal fit at `maxfev = 20000`:

| True shape of the person | ms per bimodal fit |
|---|---|
| `bimodal` | 11 |
| `unimodal` | 118 |
| `monotone` | 187 |
| `flat` | **397** |

Since these fits are only ever compared to one another through their residual
sum of squares, there is no need to pin the parameters down to eight decimal
places. `FIT_TOL = 1e-4` reproduces every error rate in this document to within
the Monte Carlo margin while running about **20 times faster**:

| Setting | ms/person | bimodal correct | uni→bi | mono→bi | flat→bi |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `maxfev=20000`, default tol | 477 | 78.5 | 15.5 | 8.0 | 11.0 |
| `FIT_TOL = 1e-5` | 93 | 78.5 | 13.0 | 6.5 | 11.0 |
| `FIT_TOL = 1e-4` | 22 | 79.0 | 10.5 | 6.0 | 10.0 |

(800 people, 30 judgments, separation 1.0; the Monte Carlo margin on each rate
is ±6.9 points.) Tighten `FIT_TOL` if you want to re-verify; expect the render
to take roughly twenty times longer.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Lower bound on fitted peak width

With `n` midpoints spread over `MID_HI - MID_LO`, neighbouring x-values are about
`(MID_HI - MID_LO) / (n - 1)` apart — 0.16 stars at 20 points. A fitted peak
narrower than that gap can sit on top of a **single lucky dot** and claim to be a
peak, which is a false-positive engine. `TIE_W_TO_GRID` sets the lower bound on
fitted width to just over the grid spacing, so a "peak" has to be supported by at
least a couple of adjacent points.
:::

```{python}
#| label: classifier

SHAPE_ORDER = ['flat', 'monotone', 'unimodal', 'bimodal']
REF_ORDER   = [0, 1, 2]

def n_ref(shape):
    """Curve shape -> number of reference points (the research question)."""
    return N_REFPOINTS[shape]

def m_flat(x, a):              return a + 0 * x
def m_mono(x, a, b):           return a + b * x
def m_uni(x, a, A, m, w):      return a + A * _bump(x, m, w)
def m_bi(x, a, A, m1, m2, w):  return a + A * (_bump(x, m1, w) + _bump(x, m2, w))

INF = np.inf

def w_floor(x):
    """Smallest fitted peak half-width we are willing to believe."""
    if not TIE_W_TO_GRID:
        return 0.08
    u = np.unique(x)
    spacing = float(np.min(np.diff(u))) if len(u) > 1 else 0.08
    return max(0.08, 0.75 * spacing)

def candidates(x):
    wlo = w_floor(x)
    return {
        'flat':     (m_flat, 1, ([-INF], [INF])),
        'monotone': (m_mono, 2, ([-INF, -INF], [INF, INF])),
        'unimodal': (m_uni,  4, ([-INF, 0, MID_LO, wlo], [INF, INF, MID_HI, 1.2])),
        'bimodal':  (m_bi,   5, ([-INF, 0, MID_LO, MID_LO, wlo],
                                 [INF, INF, MID_HI, MID_HI, 1.2])),
    }

FIT_FAILURES = {}

def _p0(x, y, shape):
    lo, amp = float(np.min(y)), float(np.ptp(y))
    span = MID_HI - MID_LO
    return {'flat':     [float(np.mean(y))],
            'monotone': [float(np.mean(y)), 0.0],
            'unimodal': [lo, amp, float(np.mean(x)), PEAK_W],
            'bimodal':  [lo, amp, MID_LO + span / 3, MID_LO + 2 * span / 3, PEAK_W]}[shape]

def info_criterion(rss, n, k, rule=None):
    """Penalised badness-of-fit. Lower is better. `k` = number of parameters."""
    rule = IC_RULE if rule is None else rule
    if n - k - 1 <= 0:
        return np.inf                     # not enough data to identify this shape
    fit = n * np.log(rss / n + 1e-12)     # how badly the shape misses the dots
    if rule == 'AIC':
        return fit + 2 * k
    if rule == 'AICc':
        return fit + 2 * k + (2 * k * (k + 1)) / (n - k - 1)
    if rule == 'BIC':
        return fit + k * np.log(n)        # steeper penalty -> more sceptical
    raise ValueError(rule)

def classify_shape(x, y):
    """Return (best shape label, fitted peak locations)."""
    best, best_ic, best_pk = 'flat', np.inf, ()
    for name, (fn, k, bnds) in candidates(x).items():
        try:
            popt, _ = curve_fit(fn, x, y, p0=_p0(x, y, name), bounds=bnds,
                                maxfev=FIT_MAXFEV, ftol=FIT_TOL, xtol=FIT_TOL)
            ic = info_criterion(float(np.sum((y - fn(x, *popt)) ** 2)), len(x), k)
        except Exception:
            # count failures rather than swallow them: a shape that never fits
            # looks identical to a shape that never wins
            FIT_FAILURES[name] = FIT_FAILURES.get(name, 0) + 1
            continue
        if ic < best_ic:
            best_ic, best = ic, name
            best_pk = (tuple(popt[2:3]) if name == 'unimodal'
                       else tuple(np.sort(popt[2:4])) if name == 'bimodal' else ())
    return best, best_pk
```

## 6b. Minimum residual error is not a selection rule

This is the natural first approach, and it fails. The reason is worth setting
out, because it motivates everything that follows.

**Residual error can only go down when you add parameters.** The `bimodal` shape
contains the `unimodal` shape as a special case (set the two peaks on top of each
other), which contains `flat` as a special case (set the amplitude to zero). So a
bimodal fit can always match whatever unimodal does, and then use its spare
freedom to chase noise a little further. Its error is **mathematically
guaranteed** to be less than or equal to the simpler shape's, whatever the data —
even for a person with no structure at all.

Picking the smallest error therefore picks `bimodal` almost every time. It is not
a test; it is a foregone conclusion.

The fix is to charge rent for parameters. All three rules below add a penalty to
the error, differing only in how steep the penalty is:

- **AIC** adds `2k`, where `k` is the number of parameters
- **AICc** adds a bit more, sized for small samples — the right default when a
  person contributes 20-45 points
- **BIC** adds `k log n`, which is a **steeper** penalty and so is more sceptical
  of complicated shapes

```{python}
#| label: tbl-selection-rules
#| tbl-cap: "The same fitted curves, scored four different ways. Each cell is the percentage of people called bimodal. A perfect rule would read 0, 0, 0, 100 across the row. 'Min RSS' is the smallest-error idea; note that it calls most people with NO structure whatsoever bimodal."

SEL_NPT, SEL_SEP, SEL_NPER = 30, 1.0, 300

def fit_all(x, y):
    """Residual sum of squares and parameter count for every candidate shape."""
    out = {}
    for name, (fn, k, bnds) in candidates(x).items():
        try:
            popt, _ = curve_fit(fn, x, y, p0=_p0(x, y, name), bounds=bnds,
                                maxfev=FIT_MAXFEV, ftol=FIT_TOL, xtol=FIT_TOL)
            out[name] = (float(np.sum((y - fn(x, *popt)) ** 2)), k)
        except Exception:
            out[name] = (np.inf, k)
    out['_n'] = len(x)
    return out

def pick(f, rule):
    n, best, best_v = f['_n'], None, np.inf
    for name in SHAPE_ORDER:
        rss, k = f[name]
        if not np.isfinite(rss):
            continue
        ll = n * np.log(rss / n + 1e-12)
        v = {'min RSS (no penalty)': rss,
             'AIC':  ll + 2 * k,
             'AICc': ll + 2 * k + (2 * k * (k + 1)) / (n - k - 1) if n - k - 1 > 0 else np.inf,
             'BIC':  ll + k * np.log(n)}[rule]
        if v < best_v:
            best_v, best = v, name
    return best

sel_fits = {sh: [fit_all(*simulate_person(sh, SEL_NPT, SEL_SEP)[:2])
                 for _ in range(SEL_NPER)] for sh in SHAPE_ORDER}

rows = []
for rule in ['min RSS (no penalty)', 'AIC', 'AICc', 'BIC']:
    r = {'selection rule': rule}
    for sh in SHAPE_ORDER:
        r[f'true {sh}'] = round(100 * np.mean(
            [pick(f, rule) == 'bimodal' for f in sel_fits[sh]]), 1)
    r['overall correct'] = round(100 * np.mean(
        [pick(f, rule) == sh for sh in SHAPE_ORDER for f in sel_fits[sh]]), 1)
    rows.append(r)
print(f"{SEL_NPER} people per true shape, {SEL_NPT} judgments, separation {SEL_SEP}")
print("cells are % CALLED BIMODAL; last column is overall accuracy")
print("")
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('selection rule')
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-rss-monotone
#| tbl-cap: "Mean residual error of each candidate shape, computed only on people whose true curve is FLAT -- no peak, no slope, nothing. Error falls steadily as parameters are added, which is why the smallest-error rule is not a test of anything."

pd.DataFrame([{'candidate shape': nm,
               'parameters (k)': sel_fits['flat'][0][nm][1],
               'mean residual error': round(float(np.mean(
                   [f[nm][0] for f in sel_fits['flat']])), 0)}
              for nm in SHAPE_ORDER]).set_index('candidate shape')
```

**How to read this.** Your binding constraint is false positives — inventing a
neutral zone that is not there. Those are the first three columns, and they are
the ones to minimise. Detection is the fourth column.

`BIC` is the most conservative of the three penalties and buys a real reduction
in false positives for a modest cost in detection. Given that a fabricated
"two reference point" subgroup is the failure mode you most want to avoid,
**`IC_RULE` is set to `'BIC'`, and every other table in this document is computed
under it.** Set it to `'AICc'` or `'AIC'` in the config block and re-render to
see the whole document change.

None of these are hypothesis tests. They are *model comparisons*: they always
return a winner, and they never tell you whether the winner is any good. That
limitation is exactly what §13 addresses.

## 6c. Peak distance as a decision statistic

This approach fails, for a reason that clarifies what the information criterion
contributes.

If you fit the two-peak shape you get two locations back, so their distance is
always computable. The problem is that **it is always computable**: fit the
two-peak shape to someone with one peak and it still returns two numbers. The
fit's natural way to imitate a single hump is to slide the two peaks on top of
each other, so most one-peak people give a small distance — but a sizeable
minority give a large one, because the fit has chased noise into two separate
bumps.

The same objection applies to **trough depth**, and to **distance divided by the
fitted peak width**, which is the scale-free version of the same idea.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-stat-showdown
#| tbl-cap: "Four ways to decide 'does this person have two reference points?'. Each statistic's threshold is set at the 95th percentile of the one-peak group, so all four are held to the SAME 5% Type I error and the comparison is fair. Cells are TYPE II ERROR -- lower is better, and power is 100 minus each."

SHOW_NPER, SHOW_NPT = 300, 45

def _peak_stats(x, y):
    """Distance, trough depth, distance/width, and the BIC gain, for one person."""
    n = len(x)
    fits = candidates(x)
    out = {}
    try:
        fn, k, bnds = fits['bimodal']
        po, _ = curve_fit(fn, x, y, p0=_p0(x, y, 'bimodal'), bounds=bnds,
                          maxfev=FIT_MAXFEV, ftol=FIT_TOL, xtol=FIT_TOL)
        b, A, m1, m2, w = po
        m1, m2 = sorted((m1, m2))
        rss = float(np.sum((y - fn(x, *po)) ** 2))
        bic_bi = info_criterion(rss, n, k, rule='BIC')
        gg = np.linspace(MID_LO, MID_HI, 1200)
        c = fn(gg, *po)
        top = c.max()
        inner = c[(gg >= m1) & (gg <= m2)]
        trough = inner.min() if len(inner) else top
        out['distance'] = m2 - m1
        out['trough depth'] = 100 * (top - trough) / max(top - b, 1e-9)
        out['distance / width'] = (m2 - m1) / max(w, 1e-9)
    except Exception:
        return None
    try:
        fn2, k2, bnds2 = fits['unimodal']
        po2, _ = curve_fit(fn2, x, y, p0=_p0(x, y, 'unimodal'), bounds=bnds2,
                           maxfev=FIT_MAXFEV, ftol=FIT_TOL, xtol=FIT_TOL)
        bic_uni = info_criterion(float(np.sum((y - fn2(x, *po2)) ** 2)), n, k2, rule='BIC')
    except Exception:
        bic_uni = np.inf
    out['BIC gain'] = bic_uni - bic_bi          # positive favours two peaks
    return out

STAT_KEYS = ['distance', 'trough depth', 'distance / width', 'BIC gain']
uni_stats = [s for s in (_peak_stats(*simulate_person('unimodal', SHOW_NPT, 1.0)[:2])
                         for _ in range(SHOW_NPER)) if s]
thr = {k: np.percentile([u[k] for u in uni_stats], 95) for k in STAT_KEYS}

show_rows = []
for sep in (0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2):
    bi_stats = [s for s in (_peak_stats(*simulate_person('bimodal', SHOW_NPT, sep)[:2])
                            for _ in range(SHOW_NPER)) if s]
    r = {'true separation': sep}
    for k in STAT_KEYS:
        r[k] = round(100 * (1 - np.mean([b[k] > thr[k] for b in bi_stats])), 1)
    show_rows.append(r)
print(f"{SHOW_NPER} people per group, {SHOW_NPT} judgments, Type I fixed at 5%.")
print("thresholds: " + ", ".join(f"{k} > {thr[k]:.2f}" for k in STAT_KEYS))
print("")
pd.DataFrame(show_rows).set_index('true separation')
```

**The single-number statistics are unusable, and the reason is the tail.** To hold
the Type I error at 5%, the threshold sits at the 95th percentile of what
one-peak people produce — and that turns out to be a fitted distance of about
1.3 stars, *wider than most of the real neutral zones you are trying to detect*.
Demanding more than that misses nearly everyone.

**Why BIC does so much better.** A distance of 1.0 stars pinned down tightly and a
distance of 1.0 stars barely constrained by the data are completely different
pieces of evidence, and the raw distance cannot tell them apart — it reports the
estimate and discards the uncertainty. BIC compares how much *better the whole
curve fits* once you pay for two extra parameters, so a wobbly, ill-determined
pair of peaks earns nothing. It weighs the evidence rather than reporting a
point estimate.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Estimand versus test statistic

- **Peak distance is the *estimand*** — it is the neutral-zone width, the number
  your paper is about, and the thing to report.
- **BIC is the *test*** — it decides whether that number is supported by this
  person's data at all.

Use BIC to decide, then report the distance for the people it selects. Using the
distance to decide as well is what fails.
:::


## 7. One population, one confusion matrix

### The generative pipeline for a single participant

The figure below walks a single simulated participant through the whole pipeline,
left to right. Every number in this document comes from repeating these four
steps a few hundred times and counting how often step 4 gets step 1 right.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pipeline
#| fig-cap: "How one simulated person is produced and then analysed. Step 1 draws that person's own parameters from the population. Step 2 turns those into a smooth, noiseless curve -- the ground truth, which exists only inside the computer. Step 3 reads the curve at the midpoints you actually test and adds slider noise; this is the only thing a real study would ever see. Step 4 hands those dots to the classifier, which never sees the dashed line."
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 3.4

PIPE_SEP, PIPE_NPT = 1.0, 30
_pr = np.random.default_rng(7)

# ---- step 1: this person's parameters, drawn from the population ----------
_draws = [draw_person_params('bimodal', PIPE_SEP) for _ in range(3000)]
_locs = [d['loc1'] for d in _draws] + [d['loc2'] for d in _draws]
p_demo = draw_person_params('bimodal', PIPE_SEP)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(13, 3.4))

ax[0].hist(_locs, bins=45, color='#bbbbbb')
for L, c in ((p_demo['loc1'], '#d62728'), (p_demo['loc2'], '#d62728')):
    ax[0].axvline(L, color=c, lw=2)
ax[0].set_title("1. draw this participant's\nreference points from the population", fontsize=9)
ax[0].set_xlabel('star rating', fontsize=8)
ax[0].set_ylabel('how common, across people', fontsize=8)
ax[0].set_yticks([])

xs_p = np.linspace(MID_LO, MID_HI, 400)
truth = np.clip(true_curve(xs_p, 'bimodal', p_demo), 0, SLIDER_MAX)
ax[1].plot(xs_p, truth, color='crimson', ls='--', lw=2)
for L in (p_demo['loc1'], p_demo['loc2']):
    ax[1].axvline(L, color='grey', lw=.8, alpha=.7)
ax[1].set_title("2. their true curve\n(never observed)", fontsize=9)

x_d = np.linspace(MID_LO, MID_HI, PIPE_NPT)
y_d = np.clip(true_curve(x_d, 'bimodal', p_demo) + _pr.normal(0, SLIDER_SD, PIPE_NPT),
              0, SLIDER_MAX)
ax[2].plot(xs_p, truth, color='crimson', ls='--', lw=1.2, alpha=.55)
ax[2].vlines(x_d, np.clip(true_curve(x_d, 'bimodal', p_demo), 0, SLIDER_MAX), y_d,
             color='#999999', lw=.8)
ax[2].scatter(x_d, y_d, s=22, color='#1f77b4', zorder=3)
ax[2].set_title(f"3. measure at {PIPE_NPT} midpoints,\nadd slider noise", fontsize=9)

lab, _pk = classify_shape(x_d, y_d)
fn, k, bnds = candidates(x_d)[lab]
try:
    popt, _ = curve_fit(fn, x_d, y_d, p0=_p0(x_d, y_d, lab), bounds=bnds,
                        maxfev=FIT_MAXFEV, ftol=FIT_TOL, xtol=FIT_TOL)
    ax[3].plot(xs_p, fn(xs_p, *popt), color='#2ca02c', lw=2)
except Exception:
    pass
ax[3].scatter(x_d, y_d, s=22, color='#1f77b4', zorder=3, alpha=.6)
ok = 'CORRECT' if lab == 'bimodal' else 'WRONG'
ax[3].set_title(f"4. classifier fits and picks:\n\"{lab}\"  ({ok})", fontsize=9)

for a in ax:
    a.set_xlim(MID_LO, MID_HI)
    a.tick_params(labelsize=7)
for a in ax[1:]:
    a.set_ylim(0, SLIDER_MAX)
    a.set_xlabel('pair midpoint', fontsize=8)
ax[1].set_ylabel('perceived difference', fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Two features of this pipeline are worth making explicit:

- **The dashed red line is the answer sheet.** It exists in step 2 and is used
  again only in step 4, to mark the classifier right or wrong. The classifier
  itself is never shown it. In a real study it does not exist at all.
- **Step 3 is the entire real study.** Those blue dots are what a participant
  actually gives you. Everything this document measures is about how much can be
  recovered from them.


```{python}
#| label: tbl-confusion
#| tbl-cap: "Confusion matrix for a single condition, as row percentages. Rows are the true shape, columns are what the classifier said. The diagonal is correct classification; everything off it is an error."

def classify_population(pop, classifier=classify_shape):
    """Classify every person ONCE and return (true, predicted) pairs."""
    return [(s, classifier(x, y)[0]) for s, x, y in pop]

def confusion_from_pairs(pairs):
    d = pd.DataFrame(pairs, columns=['true', 'pred'])
    cm = pd.crosstab(d['true'], d['pred'], normalize='index') * 100
    return cm.reindex(index=[o for o in SHAPE_ORDER if o in cm.index],
                      columns=[o for o in SHAPE_ORDER if o in cm.columns]).fillna(0)

def confusion(pop, classifier=classify_shape):
    return confusion_from_pairs(classify_population(pop, classifier))

def ref_confusion(pairs):
    """The 3x3 matrix that answers the actual question: 0, 1 or 2 reference points."""
    d = pd.DataFrame([(n_ref(t), n_ref(p)) for t, p in pairs],
                     columns=['true', 'pred'])
    cm = pd.crosstab(d['true'], d['pred'], normalize='index') * 100
    return cm.reindex(index=[r for r in REF_ORDER if r in cm.index],
                      columns=[r for r in REF_ORDER if r in cm.columns]).fillna(0)

def ref_rates(pairs):
    """The two headline numbers, weighted by how common each truth is.

    false positive = P(method says TWO | person really has none or one)
    false negative = P(method says none or one | person really has TWO)
    """
    t = np.array([n_ref(a) for a, _ in pairs])
    p = np.array([n_ref(b) for _, b in pairs])
    not2, is2 = t != 2, t == 2
    fp = 100 * np.mean(p[not2] == 2) if not2.any() else np.nan
    fn = 100 * np.mean(p[is2] != 2) if is2.any() else np.nan
    return fp, fn

DEMO_SEP = 1.0
demo_pop = simulate_population(N_PEOPLE, 20, DEMO_SEP)
cm_demo = confusion(demo_pop)
print(f"{N_PEOPLE} people, 20 judgments each, peaks {DEMO_SEP} stars apart, "
      f"peak/noise = {PEAK_AMP / SLIDER_SD:.2f}, monotone people are {MONO_DIR}")
cm_demo.round(1)
```

```{python}
#| label: read-confusion

def cell(cm, r, c):
    return float(cm.loc[r, c]) if r in cm.index and c in cm.columns else 0.0

print("Three separate routes to a false 'two reference points' claim:\n")
print(f"  flat     people called bimodal : {cell(cm_demo,'flat','bimodal'):5.1f}%")
print(f"  monotone people called bimodal : {cell(cm_demo,'monotone','bimodal'):5.1f}%")
print(f"  unimodal people called bimodal : {cell(cm_demo,'unimodal','bimodal'):5.1f}%")
print("\nThey pool into the false-positive rate below, weighted by SHAPE_MIX.")
```

The table above is the **mechanism**. The table below is the **answer**: it
collapses `flat` and `monotone` into "0 reference points", because those are two
different curves that give the same answer to your question.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ref-confusion
#| tbl-cap: "The matrix that answers the research question. Rows are how many reference points the person really has; columns are how many the method claimed. Row percentages, so the diagonal is correct and everything else is an error."

demo_pairs = classify_population(demo_pop)
rcm_demo = ref_confusion(demo_pairs)
rcm_demo.index.name = 'TRUE reference points'
rcm_demo.columns.name = 'method said'
rcm_demo.round(1)
```

```{python}
print(f"FALSE POSITIVE : {fp:5.1f}%   method claims TWO reference points")
print(f"                          when the person really has none or one")
```

## 7b. Illustrative misclassifications

The figure below shows individual misclassified participants drawn from the
simulation. The search draws participants until it finds one instance of each
kind of error.

In every panel: **blue dots** are the person's data, the **dashed red line** is
their true curve, and the **solid green line** is the shape the classifier chose.

```{python}
#| label: fig-error-examples
#| fig-cap: "Top row -- FALSE POSITIVES: people with no reference point or one, whom the method claims have two. Bottom row -- FALSE NEGATIVES: people who really have two, missed. The final panel is a success, for contrast. All at 30 judgments with a 1.0-star neutral zone."

ERR_NPT, ERR_SEP = 30, 1.0

def _fit_curve(x, y, lab, grid):
    fn, k, bnds = candidates(x)[lab]
    try:
        po, _ = curve_fit(fn, x, y, p0=_p0(x, y, lab), bounds=bnds,
                          maxfev=FIT_MAXFEV, ftol=FIT_TOL, xtol=FIT_TOL)
        return fn(grid, *po)
    except Exception:
        return None

def find_case(true_shape, want_pred, tries=4000):
    """Draw people until one is classified as `want_pred`."""
    for _ in range(tries):
        x, y, p = simulate_person(true_shape, ERR_NPT, ERR_SEP)
        lab, _ = classify_shape(x, y)
        if lab == want_pred:
            return x, y, p, lab
    return None

WANTED = [
    ('flat',     'bimodal',  'FALSE POSITIVE\ntruly 0 reference points'),
    ('monotone', 'bimodal',  'FALSE POSITIVE\ntruly 0 (Weber slope only)'),
    ('unimodal', 'bimodal',  'FALSE POSITIVE\ntruly 1 reference point'),
    ('bimodal',  'flat',     'FALSE NEGATIVE\ntruly 2, called 0'),
    ('bimodal',  'monotone', 'FALSE NEGATIVE\ntruly 2, called 0'),
    ('bimodal',  'unimodal', 'FALSE NEGATIVE\ntruly 2, called 1'),
]
grid = np.linspace(MID_LO, MID_HI, 400)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(12, 6.4), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, (ts, wp, title) in zip(axes.ravel(), WANTED):
    case = find_case(ts, wp)
    if case is None:
        ax.text(.5, .5, f"no {ts} person was\never called {wp}\nin 4000 draws",
                ha='center', va='center', transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=9)
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9)
        continue
    x, y, p, lab = case
    ax.scatter(x, y, s=20, color='#1f77b4', zorder=3, alpha=.85)
    ax.plot(grid, np.clip(true_curve(grid, ts, p), 0, SLIDER_MAX),
            color='crimson', ls='--', lw=1.6)
    fc = _fit_curve(x, y, lab, grid)
    if fc is not None:
        ax.plot(grid, fc, color='#2ca02c', lw=2)
    if ts == 'bimodal':
        for L in (p['loc1'], p['loc2']):
            ax.axvline(L, color='grey', lw=.8, alpha=.5)
    ax.set_title(f"{title}\nmethod said: {lab}", fontsize=9)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)

# one success, for contrast
succ = find_case('bimodal', 'bimodal')
if succ:
    x, y, p, lab = succ
    ax = axes[1, 2]
    ax.clear()
    ax.scatter(x, y, s=20, color='#1f77b4', zorder=3, alpha=.85)
    ax.plot(grid, np.clip(true_curve(grid, 'bimodal', p), 0, SLIDER_MAX),
            color='crimson', ls='--', lw=1.6)
    fc = _fit_curve(x, y, 'bimodal', grid)
    if fc is not None:
        ax.plot(grid, fc, color='#2ca02c', lw=2)
    for L in (p['loc1'], p['loc2']):
        ax.axvline(L, color='grey', lw=.8, alpha=.5)
    ax.set_title("CORRECT\ntruly 2, found 2", fontsize=9)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)

axes[0, 0].set_ylim(0, SLIDER_MAX)
for ax in axes[1]:
    ax.set_xlabel('pair midpoint', fontsize=8)
for ax in axes[:, 0]:
    ax.set_ylabel('perceived difference', fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

**Top row.** The fitted curves are plausible descriptions of the data. A false
positive is not a failure of the fitting procedure; it is a configuration of
noise that resembles two humps. Nothing in the data distinguishes these
participants from genuine two-reference-point cases. This is why the false-positive rate
cannot be reduced to zero by refining the estimator, and why the complexity
penalty in §6b is load-bearing.

**Bottom row.** Missed participants typically have one peak swamped by
noise, or the trough between their peaks filled in by a few high dots. Compare
the last panel: the successes are visibly two-humped and the failures are not. The information is not present in the data, which is why §13.1 finds that
additional judgments do not recover it.


## 8. Sweeping judgments per participant and reference-point separation

The two knobs that genuinely move the error rates: how much data each person
gives you, and how far apart their peaks are.

```{python}
#| label: sweep

def sweep(n_points_grid, sep_grid, n_people=None, classifier=classify_shape):
    n_people = n_people or N_PEOPLE
    out = []
    for sep in sep_grid:
        for npt in n_points_grid:
            pop = simulate_population(n_people, npt, sep)
            pairs = classify_population(pop, classifier)     # classify once
            cm = confusion_from_pairs(pairs)
            fp, fn = ref_rates(pairs)
            out.append({
                'peak separation': sep, 'judgments per person': npt,
                'n people': n_people,
                'FALSE POSITIVE: said 2, truth 0 or 1 (%)': fp,
                'FALSE NEGATIVE: said 0 or 1, truth 2 (%)': fn,
                'bimodal correct (%)': cell(cm, 'bimodal', 'bimodal'),
                'unimodal called bimodal (%)': cell(cm, 'unimodal', 'bimodal'),
                'monotone called bimodal (%)': cell(cm, 'monotone', 'bimodal'),
                'unimodal correct (%)': cell(cm, 'unimodal', 'unimodal'),
                'monotone correct (%)': cell(cm, 'monotone', 'monotone'),
                'overall accuracy (%)': float(np.mean([t == p for t, p in pairs]) * 100),
            })
    return pd.DataFrame(out)

sw = sweep(N_POINTS, SEP_GRID)
if FIT_FAILURES:
    print("fit failures by shape:", FIT_FAILURES)
_n_bi = N_PEOPLE * SHAPE_MIX['bimodal']
print(f"{N_PEOPLE} people per cell, of whom about {_n_bi:.0f} are truly bimodal.")
print(f"Monte Carlo precision on a bimodal-row cell: about "
      f"+/- {1.96 * np.sqrt(0.25 / _n_bi) * 100:.1f} percentage points.")
```

These first two tables are stated directly in terms of the research question, and
pool every route to each kind of error.

::: {.callout-important}
## What is held fixed across these rows

`PEAK_W` is **fixed at its config value throughout this sweep**, so as the
reference-point separation changes down a column, the **depth of the dip changes
with it**. The rows are not separated only by how far apart the reference points
are; they also differ in how pronounced the dip between the humps is:

| separation | dip depth, as % of hump height | two humps at all? |
|---|---|---|
| 0.2 / 0.4 / 0.6 | 0% | no - single hump |
| 0.8 | 20% | yes |
| 1.0 | 50% | yes |
| 1.2 | 73% | yes |

That coupling is not a flaw — the two quantities are not independent (§5a) — but
it means a row should be read as "this separation *at this peak width*", not as
separation alone. To vary the dip depth independently, set `PEAK_W` from a target
depth using `w_for_trough` in §5a and re-render.
:::

```{python}
#| label: tbl-sweep-ref-fp
#| tbl-cap: "TYPE I ERROR / FALSE POSITIVE (lower is better): percentage of people with NO or ONE reference point whom the method claims have TWO. Rows are peak separation in star units; columns are judgments per person."

sw.pivot_table(index='peak separation', columns='judgments per person',
               values='FALSE POSITIVE: said 2, truth 0 or 1 (%)').round(1)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-sweep-ref-fn
#| tbl-cap: "TYPE II ERROR / FALSE NEGATIVE (lower is better): percentage of people who really have TWO reference points whom the method claims have none or one. Power is 100 minus this. Rows where section 2 shows a single-humped true curve are NOT method failures -- those people do have two reference points, but this task cannot render them as two peaks. Read those rows as the cost of the design, and see section 11 for a design without that floor."

sw.pivot_table(index='peak separation', columns='judgments per person',
               values='FALSE NEGATIVE: said 0 or 1, truth 2 (%)').round(1)
```

The remaining tables in this section break those two numbers down by curve shape,
which is useful for diagnosing *why* an error rate is what it is.

Rows are peak separation in star units; columns are judgments per person. Compare against the 'this task can see it?' column in section 2 -- rows marked 'NO' there have two reference points but only one hump, so there is no second peak available to find."

```{python}
#| label: fig-sweep

for sep, g in sw.groupby('peak separation'):
    g = g.sort_values('judgments per person')

                 lw=1.8 if real else 1.0, ls='-' if real else ':')

    axes[1].plot(g['judgments per person'], g['unimodal called bimodal (%)'],

axes[0].axhline(80, color='crimson', ls='--', lw=1)

for ax in axes:
```

## 8b. Interactive parameter explorer

The tables above fix most settings and vary one or two. This does the opposite:
pick any combination and see both error rates at once.

Move the two dropdowns. The **grey band** marks neutral zones narrower than
`2 × PEAK_W`, where the two reference points produce a single hump and there is nothing
to detect (§5) — a high false-negative rate inside that band is the correct
answer, not a failure.

```{python}
#| label: widget-explorer
#| echo: false

import json, os
from IPython.display import HTML, display

if not os.path.exists('error_grid.csv'):

else:

        'judg': sorted(_g['judgments'].unique().tolist()),
        'seps': sorted(_g['separation'].unique().tolist()),
        'floor': 2 * PEAK_W,
        'n_not2': int(_g['n_not2'].iloc[0]),
        'n_is2': int(_g['n_is2'].iloc[0]),
    })
    _html = """
<div id="expl" style="font-family:system-ui,-apple-system,sans-serif;max-width:760px;
     border:1px solid #d8d8d8;border-radius:8px;padding:14px 16px;background:#fcfcfc">
  <div style="display:flex;gap:26px;flex-wrap:wrap;align-items:flex-end;margin-bottom:6px">
    <label style="font-size:13px">Signal vs noise (PEAK_AMP / SLIDER_SD)<br>
      <select id="ex_ratio" style="font-size:14px;padding:3px 6px;margin-top:3px"></select>
    </label>
    <label style="font-size:13px">Judgments per person<br>
      <select id="ex_judg" style="font-size:14px;padding:3px 6px;margin-top:3px"></select>
    </label>
    <div id="ex_read" style="font-size:13px;line-height:1.5"></div>
  </div>
  <svg id="ex_svg" viewBox="0 0 700 330" style="width:100%;height:auto"></svg>
  <p id="ex_note" style="font-size:11.5px;color:#666;margin:2px 0 0"></p>
</div>
<script>
(function(){
  var D = __PAYLOAD__;
  var svg = document.getElementById('ex_svg'),
      selR = document.getElementById('ex_ratio'),
      selJ = document.getElementById('ex_judg'),
      read = document.getElementById('ex_read'),
      note = document.getElementById('ex_note');
  D.ratios.forEach(function(r){ var o=document.createElement('option');
    o.value=r; o.textContent=r.toFixed(1); if(r===2.5) o.selected=true; selR.appendChild(o); });
  D.judg.forEach(function(j){ var o=document.createElement('option');
    o.value=j; o.textContent=j; if(j===45) o.selected=true; selJ.appendChild(o); });

  var L=58, R=18, T=16, B=44, W=700, H=330;
  var x0=L, x1=W-R, y0=H-B, y1=T;
  var sMin=Math.min.apply(null,D.seps), sMax=Math.max.apply(null,D.seps);
  function px(s){ return x0 + (s-sMin)/(sMax-sMin)*(x1-x0); }
  function py(v){ return y0 - (v/100)*(y0-y1); }
  function el(n,a){ var e=document.createElementNS('http://www.w3.org/2000/svg',n);
    for(var k in a) e.setAttribute(k,a[k]); return e; }

  function draw(){
    var r=parseFloat(selR.value), j=parseInt(selJ.value);
    var rows=D.rows.filter(function(d){return d.peak_noise===r && d.judgments===j;})
                   .sort(function(a,b){return a.separation-b.separation;});
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);

    var fx=px(Math.min(D.floor,sMax));
    if(fx>x0) svg.appendChild(el('rect',{x:x0,y:y1,width:fx-x0,height:y0-y1,
      fill:'#999',opacity:0.13}));
    if(fx>x0+8) { var ft=el('text',{x:(x0+fx)/2,y:y1+14,'text-anchor':'middle',
      'font-size':10,fill:'#777'}); ft.textContent='one hump — nothing to detect';
      svg.appendChild(ft); }

    [0,20,40,60,80,100].forEach(function(v){
      svg.appendChild(el('line',{x1:x0,x2:x1,y1:py(v),y2:py(v),
        stroke:'#e4e4e4','stroke-width':1}));

      t.textContent=v+'%'; svg.appendChild(t);

      t.textContent=s.toFixed(1); svg.appendChild(t);

    var xl=el('text',{x:(x0+x1)/2,y:H-8,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':12,fill:'#333'});
    xl.textContent='neutral-zone width (stars)'; svg.appendChild(xl);

    function series(key,color,label){
      var pts=rows.map(function(d){return px(d.separation)+','+py(d[key]);}).join(' ');
      svg.appendChild(el('polyline',{points:pts,fill:'none',stroke:color,'stroke-width':2.4}));
      rows.forEach(function(d){

      });

    var best=rows.filter(function(d){return d.separation>D.floor && d.type2<=20;});
    read.innerHTML = '<b>At these settings</b><br>' +

    note.textContent='Dashed red line marks a 20% Type II error (80% power). '+
      'Each point uses about '+D.n_not2+' people with 0 or 1 reference points and '+
      D.n_is2+' with 2, so the margin is roughly ±5 points.';
  }
  selR.addEventListener('change',draw);
  selJ.addEventListener('change',draw);
```
